query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is primarily governed by the multilayer interfaces, which act as effective barriers to dislocation climb and lattice diffusion. These interfaces interrupt dislocation motion and impede creep mechanisms, leading to a slower time-dependent deformation compared to homogeneous (monolithic) coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings fabricated as multilayer films with alternating layers (e.g., via magnetron sputtering or laser cladding) that exhibit well-defined interfaces and minimal short-range ordering effects.
generation.intervention: Subject both multilayer HEA coatings and identically composed monolithic HEA coatings to long-term, constant-load or nanoindentation creep tests at controlled temperatures (e.g., up to ~573 K) in an inert environment.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under static or low strain-rate conditions in an inert atmosphere to eliminate environmental (oxidation) effects, ensuring that temperature and applied stress are systematically controlled.
generation.structural_mediator: The physical barrier provided by the multilayer interfaces, which disrupt dislocation propagation and inhibit diffusion‐mediated dislocation climb through local strain partitioning.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load, dislocations in HEA coatings tend to move by climb and glide. In multilayer structures the numerous interfaces force dislocations to repeatedly change direction or become pinned, raising the effective activation energy for creep. This results in reduced time-dependent plastic deformation relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer HEA coatings will demonstrate a significantly lower creep rate and reduced time-dependent plastic strain compared to their monolithic counterparts under identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous (monolithic) HEA coating with the same overall composition and processing history but lacking internal multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be most pronounced in coatings operating over a moderate temperature range (ambient to ~573 K) and under stresses typical for protective applications, where dislocation-mediated creep predominates over other high-temperature mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While the interface blocking mechanism is anticipated to be dominant, the precise quantitative contribution of interface structure versus residual stresses or minor compositional variations remains to be fully isolated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one set of multilayer HEA coatings with sharp, well-defined interfaces and another set fabricated as homogeneous monolithic HEA coatings. Perform nanoindentation creep tests or constant-load deformation experiments under identical conditions (temperature, stress, environment) while imaging microstructural evolution (e.g., via TEM or in situ SEM).
measurements: Creep displacement (strain vs. time) under constant load
Microstructural evolution at interfaces (dislocation activity, interface integrity)
Activation energy for creep from strain rate sensitivity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep rate (i.e., time-dependent plastic deformation) compared to the homogeneous coatings, or if no observable dislocation pile-up or interface pinning is detected at the multilayer boundaries, then the hypothesis that interfaces are the dominant mechanism for creep resistance is falsified.

The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Additionally, the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction are found to critically affect the alloy’s creep resistance. The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol−1, whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol−1. Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M23C6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
